entries.3d3bf6ad4d5e4cbbbdd6a072e46904068bbf5b0b: <div sID="gen31868" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Eph.5" sID="Eph.5"/> <div eID="gen31868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31869" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31870" type="x-p"/> We had several important exhortations in the close of the foregoing chapter, and they are continued in this: particularly, I. We have here an exhortation to mutual love and charity, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.1-Eph.5.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. Against all manner of uncleanness, with proper arguments and remedies proposed against such sins: and some further cautions are added, and other duties recommended, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.3-Eph.5.20">ver. 3-20</reference>. III. The apostle directs to the conscientious discharge of relative duties, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.21-Eph.6.9">from ver. 21</reference>, throughout this, and in the beginning of the next chapter.
entries.2ba96fa9b6268dffc861035fd0687f50d32767dc: <div eID="gen31870" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31869" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions against Impurity. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31871" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children; <hi type="super">2</hi> And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour. <div eID="gen31871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31872" type="x-p"/> Here we have the exhortation to mutual love, or to Christian charity. The apostle had been insisting on this in the former chapter, and particularly in the <reference osisRef="Eph.4.17-Eph.4.32">last verses</reference> of it, to which the particle <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> refers, and connects what he had said there with what is contained in these verses, thus: "Because God, for Christ's sake, has forgiven you, therefore be you followers of God, or <hi type="italic">imitators</hi> of him;" for so the word signifies. Pious persons should imitate the God whom they worship, as far as he has revealed himself as imitable by them. They must conform themselves to his example, and have his image renewed upon them. This puts a great honour upon practical religion, that it is the imitating of God. We must be holy as God is holy, merciful as he is merciful, perfect as he is perfect. But there is no one attribute of God more recommended to our imitation than that of his goodness. Be you imitators of God, or resemble him, in every grace, and especially in his love, and in his pardoning goodness. God <hi type="italic">is love; and those that dwell in love dwell in God and God in them.</hi> Thus he has proclaimed his name, <hi type="italic">Gracious and merciful, and abundant in goodness. As dear children,</hi> as children (who are wont to be greatly beloved by their parents) usually resemble them in the lineaments and features of their faces, and in the dispositions and qualities of their minds; or as becomes the children of God, who are beloved and cherished by their heavenly Father. Children are obliged to imitate their parents in what is good, especially when dearly beloved by them. The character that we bear of God's children obliges us to resemble him, especially in his love and goodness, in his mercy and readiness to forgive. And those only are God's dear children who imitate him in these. It follows, <hi type="italic">And walk in love,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">v. 2</reference>. This godlike grace should conduct and influence our whole conversation, which is meant by walking in it. It should be the principle from which we act; it should direct the ends at which we aim. We should be more careful to give proof of the sincerity of our love one to another. <hi type="italic">As Christ also hath loved us.</hi> Here the apostle directs us to the example of Christ, whom Christians are obliged to imitate, and in whom we have an instance of the most free and generous love that ever was, that great love wherewith he hath loved us. We are all joint sharers in that love, and partakers of the comfort of it, and therefore should love one another, Christ having loved us all and given such proof of his love to us; for <hi type="italic">he hath given himself for us.</hi> The apostle designedly enlarges on the subject; for what can yield us more delightful matter for contemplation than this? Christ gave himself to die for us; and the death of Christ was the great sacrifice of atonement: <hi type="italic">An offering and a sacrifice to God;</hi> or an offering, even a sacrifice—a propitiatory sacrifice, to expiate our guilt, which had been prefigured in the legal oblations and sacrifices; and this <hi type="italic">for a sweet-smelling savour.</hi> Some observe that the sin-offerings were never said to be of a sweet-smelling savour; but this is said of <hi type="italic">the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.</hi> As he offered himself with a design to be accepted of God, so God did accept, was pleased with, and appeased by, that sacrifice. Note, As the sacrifice of Christ was efficacious with God, so his example should be prevailing with us, and we should carefully copy after it.
entries.57ba489416d9f24462ad9c4533d7d93e99064c74: <div eID="gen31872" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Preservatives from Impurity; Cautions and Admonitions. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31873" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints; <hi type="super">4</hi> Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks. 5 For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. <hi type="super">6</hi> Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience. <hi type="super">7</hi> Be not ye therefore partakers with them. <hi type="super">8</hi> For ye were sometimes darkness, but now <hi type="italic">are ye</hi> light in the Lord: walk as children of light: 9 (For the fruit of the Spirit <hi type="italic">is</hi> in all goodness and righteousness and truth;) <hi type="super">10</hi> Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. <hi type="super">11</hi> And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret. <hi type="super">13</hi> But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light. 14 Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light. <hi type="super">15</hi> See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, <hi type="super">16</hi> Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. <hi type="super">17</hi> Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord <hi type="italic">is.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; <hi type="super">19</hi> Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; <hi type="super">20</hi> Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; <div eID="gen31873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31874" type="x-p"/> These verses contain a caution against all manner of uncleanness, with proper remedies and arguments proposed: some further cautions are added, and other duties recommended. Filthy lusts must be suppressed, in order to the supporting of holy love. <hi type="italic">Walk in love,</hi> and <hi type="italic">shun fornication and all uncleanness. Fornication</hi> is folly committed between unmarried persons. <hi type="italic">All uncleanness</hi> includes all other sorts of filthy lusts, which were too common among the Gentiles. Or <hi type="italic">covetousness,</hi> which being thus connected, and mentioned as a thing which should not be <hi type="italic">once named,</hi> some understand it, in the chaste style of the scripture, of unnatural lust; while others take it in the more common sense, for an immoderate desire of gain or an insatiable love of riches, which is spiritual adultery; for by this the soul, which was espoused to God, goes astray from him, and embraces the bosom of a stranger, and therefore carnal worldlings are called adulterers: <hi type="italic">You adulterers and adulteresses, know you not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God?</hi> Now these sins must be dreaded and detested in the highest degree: <hi type="italic">Let it not be once named among you,</hi> never in a way of approbation nor without abhorrence, <hi type="italic">as becometh saints,</hi> holy persons, who are separated from the world, and dedicated unto God. The apostle not only cautions against the gross acts of sin, but against what some may be apt to make light of, and think to be excusable. <hi type="italic">Neither filthiness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.4">v. 4</reference>), by which may be understood all wanton and unseemly gestures and behaviour; <hi type="italic">nor foolish talking,</hi> obscene and lewd discourse, or, more generally, such vain discourse as betrays much folly and indiscretion, and is far from edifying the hearers; <hi type="italic">nor jesting.</hi> The Greek word <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eutrapelia</hi></hi> is the same which Aristotle, in his Ethics, makes a virtue: pleasantness of conversation. And there is no doubt an innocent and inoffensive jesting, which we cannot suppose the apostle here forbids. Some understand him of such scurrilous and abusive reflections as tend to expose others and to make them appear ridiculous. This is bad enough: but the context seems to restrain it to such pleasantry of discourse as is filthy and obscene, which he may also design by that <hi type="italic">corrupt,</hi> or putrid and rotten, communication that he speaks of, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.29">ch. iv. 29</reference>. Of these things he says, <hi type="italic">They are not convenient.</hi> Indeed there is more than inconvenience, even a great deal of mischief, in them. They are so far from being profitable that they pollute and poison the hearers. But the meaning is, Those things do not become Christians, and are very unsuitable to their profession and character. Christians are allowed to be cheerful and pleasant; but they must be merry and wise. The apostle adds, <hi type="italic">But rather giving of thanks:</hi> so far let the Christian's way of mirth be from that of obscene and profane wit, that he may delight his mind, and make himself cheerful, by a grateful remembrance of God's goodness and mercy to him, and by blessing and praising him on account of these. Note, 1. We should take all occasions to render thanksgivings and praises to God for his kindness and favours to us. 2. A reflection on the grace and goodness of God to us, with a design to excite our thankfulness to him, is proper to refresh and delight the Christian's mind, and to make him cheerful. Dr. Hammond thinks that <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eucharistia</hi></hi> may signify gracious, pious, religious discourse in general, by way of opposition to what the apostle condemns. Our cheerfulness, instead of breaking out into what is vain and sinful, and a profanation of God's name, should express itself as becomes Christians, and in what may tend to his glory. If men abounded more in good and pious expressions, they would not be so apt to utter ill and unbecoming words; for shall <hi type="italic">blessing</hi> and <hi type="italic">cursing,</hi> lewdness and thanksgivings, <hi type="italic">proceed out of the same mouth?</hi> <div eID="gen31874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31875" type="x-p"/> I. To fortify us against the sins of uncleanness, &c., the apostle urges several arguments, and prescribes several remedies, in what follows, <div eID="gen31875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31876" type="x-p"/> 1. He urges several arguments, As, (1.) Consider that these are sins which shut persons out of heaven: <hi type="italic">For this you know,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">v. 5</reference>. They knew it, being informed of it by the Christian religion. By <hi type="italic">a covetous man</hi> some understand a lewd lascivious libertine, who indulges himself in those vile lusts which were accounted the certain marks of a heathen and an idolater. Others understand it in the common acceptation of the word; and such a man is an idolater because there is spiritual idolatry in the love of this world. As the epicure makes a god of his belly, so the covetous man makes a god of his money, sets those affectations upon it, and places that hope, confidence, and delight, in worldly good, which should be reserved for God only. He serves mammon instead of God. Of these persons it is said that they <hi type="italic">have no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God;</hi> that is, the kingdom of Christ, who is God, or the kingdom which is God's by nature, and Christ's as he is Mediator, the kingdom which Christ has purchased and which God bestows. Heaven is here described as a kingdom (as frequently elsewhere) with respect to its eminency and glory, its fulness and sufficiency, &c. In this kingdom the saints and servants of God have an inheritance; for it is the <hi type="italic">inheritance of the saints in light.</hi> But those who are impenitent, and allow themselves either in the lusts of the flesh or the love of the world, are not Christians indeed, and so belong not to the kingdom of grace, nor shall they ever come to the kingdom of glory. Let us then be excited to be on our guard against those sins which would exclude and shut us out of heaven. (2.) These sins bring the wrath of God upon those who are guilty of them: "<hi type="italic">Let no man deceive you with vain words,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.5.6">v. 6</reference>. Let none flatter you, as though such things were tolerable and to be allowed of in Christians, or as though they were not very provoking and offensive unto God, or as though you might indulge yourselves in them and yet escape with impunity. These are <hi type="italic">vain words.</hi>" Observe, Those who flatter themselves and others with hopes of impunity in sin do but put a cheat upon themselves and others. Thus Satan deceived our first parents with vain words when he said to them, <hi type="italic">You shall not surely die.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">vain words</hi> indeed; for those who trust to them will find themselves wretchedly imposed upon, <hi type="italic">for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience.</hi> By <hi type="italic">children of disobedience</hi> may be meant the Gentiles, who disbelieved, and refused to comply with, and to submit themselves to, the gospel: or, more generally, all obstinate sinners, who will not be reclaimed, but are given over to disobedience. Disobedience is the very malignity of sin. And it is by a usual Hebraism that such sinners are called children of disobedience; and such indeed they are from their childhood, going astray as soon as they are born. <hi type="italic">The wrath of God comes upon</hi> such because of their sins; sometimes in this world, but more especially in the next. And dare we make light of that which will lay us under the wrath of God? O no. <hi type="italic">Be not you therefore partakers with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.7">v. 7</reference>. "Do not partake with them in their sins, that you may not share in their punishment." We partake with other men in their sins, not only when we live in the same sinful manner that they do, and consent and comply with their temptations and solicitations to sin, but when we encourage them in their sins, prompt them to sin, and do not prevent and hinder them, as far as it may be in our power to do so. (3.) Consider what obligations Christians are under to live at another rate than such sinners do: <hi type="italic">For you were sometimes darkness, but now,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">v. 8</reference>. The meaning is, "Such courses are very unsuitable to your present condition; for, whereas in your Gentile and your unregenerate state you were darkness, you have now undergone a great change." The apostle calls their former condition <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> in the abstract, to express the great darkness they were in. They lived wicked and profane lives, being destitute of the light of instruction without and of the illumination and grace of the blessed Spirit within. Note, A state of sin is a state of darkness. Sinners, like men in the dark, are going they know not whither, and doing they know not what. But the grace of God had produced a mighty change in their souls: <hi type="italic">Now are you light in the Lord,</hi> savingly enlightened by the word and the Spirit of God. <hi type="italic">Now,</hi> upon your believing in Christ, and your receiving the gospel. <hi type="italic">Walk as children of light.</hi> Children of light, according to the Hebrew dialect, are those who are in a state of light, endued with knowledge and holiness. "Now, being such, let your conversation be suitable to your condition and privileges, and accordingly live up to the obligation you are under by that knowledge and those advantages you enjoy—<hi type="italic">Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.10">v. 10</reference>), examining and searching diligently what God has revealed to be his will, and making it appear that you approve it by conforming yourselves to it." Observe, We must not only dread and avoid that which is displeasing to God, but enquire and consider what will be acceptable to him, searching the scriptures with this view, thus keeping at the greatest distance from these sins. <div eID="gen31876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31877" type="x-p"/> 2. The apostle prescribes some remedies against them. As, (1.) If we would not be entangled by the lusts of the flesh, we must bring forth <hi type="italic">the fruits of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.9">v. 9</reference>. This is expected from the children of light, that, being illuminated, they be also sanctified by the Spirit, and thereupon bring forth his fruit, which <hi type="italic">is in all goodness,</hi> an inclination to do good and to show mercy, <hi type="italic">and righteousness,</hi> which signifies justice in our dealings. Thus they are taken more strictly; but, more generally, all religion is goodness and righteousness. And in and with these must be <hi type="italic">truth,</hi> or sincerity and uprightness of heart. (2.) We must have no fellowship with sin nor sinners, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">v. 11</reference>. Sinful works are works of darkness: they come from the darkness of ignorance, they seek the darkness of concealment, and they lead to the darkness of hell. These works of darkness are <hi type="italic">unfruitful works;</hi> there is nothing got by them in the long run, whatever profit is pretended by sin, it will by no means balance the loss; for it issues in the utter ruin and destruction of the impenitent sinner. We must therefore <hi type="italic">have no fellowship</hi> with these unfruitful works; as we must not practise them ourselves, so we must not countenance others in the practice of them. There are many ways of our being accessary to the sins of others, by commendation, counsel, consent, or concealment. And, if we share with others in their sin, we must expect to share with them in their plagues. Nay, if we thus have fellowship with them, we shall be in the utmost danger of acting as they do ere long. But, rather than have fellowship with them, we must <hi type="italic">reprove them,</hi> implying that if we do not reprove the sins of others we have fellowship with them. We must prudently and in our places witness against the sins of others, and endeavour to convince them of their sinfulness, when we can do it seasonably and pertinently, in our words; but especially by the holiness of our lives, and a religious conversation. Reprove their sins by abounding in the contrary duties. One reason given is, <hi type="italic">For it is a shame even to speak of those things,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.5.12">v. 12</reference>. They are so filthy and abominable that it is a shame to mention them, except in a way of reproof, much more must it be a shame to have any fellowship with them. <hi type="italic">The things which are done of them in secret.</hi> The apostle seems to speak here of the Gentile idolaters, and of their horrid mysteries, which abounded with detestable wickedness, and which none were permitted to divulge upon pain of death. Observe, A good man is ashamed to speak that which many wicked people are not ashamed to act; but, as far as their wickedness appears, it should be reproved by good men. There follows another reason for such reproof: <hi type="italic">But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.13">v. 13</reference>. The meaning of this passage may be this: "All those unfruitful works of darkness which you are called upon to reprove are laid open, and made to appear in their proper colours to the sinners themselves, by the light of doctrine or of God's word in your mouths, as faithful reprovers, or by that instructive light which is diffused by the holiness of your lives and by your exemplary walk." Observe, The light of God's word, and the exemplification of it in a Christian conversation, are proper means to convince sinners of their sin and wickedness. It follows, <hi type="italic">For whatsoever doth make manifest is light;</hi> that is, it is the light that discovers what was concealed before in darkness; and accordingly it becomes those who are <hi type="italic">children of light,</hi> who are <hi type="italic">light in the Lord,</hi> to discover to others their sins, and to endeavour to convince them of the evil and danger of them, thus shining as lights in the world. The apostle further urges this duty from the example of God or Christ: <hi type="italic">Wherefore he saith,</hi> &c. (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">v. 14</reference>); as if he had said, "In doing this, you will copy after the great God, who has set himself to awaken sinners from their sleep, and to raise them from the death of sin, that they might receive light from Christ." <hi type="italic">He saith.</hi> The Lord is constantly saying in his word what is more particularly expressed in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.1">Isa. lx. 1</reference>. Or, Christ, by his ministers, who preach the everlasting gospel, is continually calling upon sinners to this effect: <hi type="italic">Awake, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead.</hi> The same thing in the main is designed by these different expressions; and they serve to remind us of the great stupidity and the wretched security of sinners, how insensible they are of their danger, and how unapt they naturally are to spiritual motions, sensations, and actions. When God calls upon them to awake, and to arise, his meaning is that they would break off their sins by repentance, and enter on a course of holy obedience, and he encourages them to essay and do their utmost that way, by that gracious promise, <hi type="italic">And Christ shall give thee light; or Christ shall enlighten thee,</hi> or <hi type="italic">shall shine upon thee.</hi> "He shall bring thee into a state of knowledge, holiness, and comfort, assisting thee with his grace, and refreshing thy mind with joy and peace here and rewarding thee with eternal glory at length." Observe, When we are endeavouring to convince sinners, and to reform them from their sins, we are imitating God and Christ in that which is their great design throughout the gospel. Some indeed understand this as a call to sinners and to saints: to sinners to repent and turn; to saints to stir up themselves to their duty. The former must arise from their spiritual death; and the latter must awake from their spiritual deadness. (3.) Another remedy against sin is circumspection, care, or caution (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">See then,</hi> &c. This may be understood either with respect to what immediately precedes, "If you are to reprove others for their sins, and would be faithful to your duty in this particular, you must look well to yourselves, and to your own behaviour and conduct" (and, indeed, those only are fit to reprove others who walk with due circumspection and care themselves): or else we have here another remedy or rather preservative from the before-mentioned sins; and this I take to be the design of the apostle, being impossible to maintain purity and holiness of heart and life without great circumspection and care. <hi type="italic">Walk circumspectly,</hi> or, as the word signifies, accurately, exactly, in the right way, in order to which we must be frequently consulting our rule, and the directions we have in the sacred oracles. <hi type="italic">Not as fools,</hi> who walk at all adventures, and who have no understanding of their duty, nor of the worth of their souls, and through neglect, supineness, and want of care, fall into sin, and destroy themselves; <hi type="italic">but as wise,</hi> as persons taught of God and endued with wisdom from above. Circumspect walking is the effect of true wisdom, but the contrary is the effect of folly. It follows, <hi type="italic">redeeming the time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">v. 16</reference>), literally, <hi type="italic">buying the opportunity.</hi> It is a metaphor taken from merchants and traders who diligently observe and improve the seasons for merchandise and trade. It is a great part of Christian wisdom to redeem the time. Good Christians must be good husbands of their time, and take care to improve it to the best of purposes, by watching against temptations, by doing good while it is in the power of their hands, and by filling it up with proper employment—one special preservative from sin. They should make the best use they can of the present seasons of grace. Our time is a talent given us by God for some good end, and it is misspent and lost when it is not employed according to his design. If we have lost our time heretofore, we must endeavour to redeem it by doubling our diligence in doing our duty for the future. The reason given is <hi type="italic">because the days are evil,</hi> either by reason of the wickedness of those who dwell in them, or rather "as they are troublesome and dangerous times to you who live in them." Those were times of persecution wherein the apostle wrote this: the Christians were in jeopardy every hour. When the days are evil we have one superadded argument to redeem time, especially because we know not how soon they may be worse. People are very apt to complain of bad times; it were well if that would stir them up to redeem time. "<hi type="italic">Wherefore,</hi>" says the apostle (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.17">v. 17</reference>), "because of the badness of the times, <hi type="italic">be you not unwise,</hi> ignorant of your duty and negligent about your souls, <hi type="italic">but understanding what the will of the Lord is.</hi> Study, consider, and further acquaint yourselves with the will of God, as determining your duty." Observe, Ignorance of our duty, and neglect of our souls, are evidences of the greatest folly; while an acquaintance with the will of God, and a care to comply with it, bespeak the best and truest wisdom. <div eID="gen31877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31878" type="x-p"/> II. In the <reference osisRef="Eph.5.18-Eph.5.20">three following verses</reference> the apostle warns against some other particular sins, and urges some other duties. 1. He warns against the sin of drunkenness: <hi type="italic">And be not drunk with wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.18">v. 18</reference>. This was a sin very frequent among the heathens; and particularly on occasion of the festivals of their gods, and more especially in their Bacchanalia: then they were wont to inflame themselves with wine, and all manner of inordinate lusts were consequent upon it: and therefore the apostle adds, <hi type="italic">wherein,</hi> or in which drunkenness, <hi type="italic">is excess.</hi> The word <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">asotia</hi></hi> may signify <hi type="italic">luxury</hi> or <hi type="italic">dissoluteness;</hi> and it is certain that drunkenness is no friend to chastity and purity of life, but it virtually contains all manner of extravagance, and transports men into gross sensuality and vile enormities. Note, Drunkenness is a sin that seldom goes alone, but often involves men in other instances of guilt: it is a sin very provoking to God, and a great hindrance to the spiritual life. The apostle may mean all such intemperance and disorder as are opposite to the sober and prudent demeanor he intends in his advice, to redeem the time. 2. Instead of being filled with wine, he exhorts them to <hi type="italic">be filled with the Spirit.</hi> Those who are full of drink are not likely to be full of the Spirit; and therefore this duty is opposed to the former sin. The meaning of the exhortation is that men should labour for a plentiful measure of the graces of the Spirit, that would fill their souls with great joy, strength, and courage, which things sensual men expect their wine should inspire them with. We cannot be guilty of any excess in our endeavours after these: nay, we ought not to be satisfied with a little of the Spirit, but to be aspiring after measures, so as to be filled with the Spirit. Now by this means we shall come to <hi type="italic">understand what the will of the Lord is;</hi> for the Spirit of God is given as a Spirit of wisdom and of understanding. And because those who are filled with the Spirit will be carried out in acts of devotion, and all the proper expressions of it, therefore the apostle exhorts, 3. To sing unto the Lord, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">v. 19</reference>. Drunkards are wont to sing obscene and profane songs. The heathens, in their Bacchanalia, used to sing hymns to Bacchus, whom they called the god of wine. Thus they expressed their joy; but the joy of Christians should express itself in songs of praise to their God. In these they should <hi type="italic">speak to themselves</hi> in their assemblies and meetings together, for mutual edification. By <hi type="italic">psalms</hi> may be meant David's psalms, or such composures as were fitly sung with musical instruments. By <hi type="italic">hymns</hi> may be meant such others as were confined to matter of praise, as those of Zacharias, Simeon, &c. <hi type="italic">Spiritual songs</hi> may contain a greater variety of matter, doctrinal, prophetical, historical, &c. Observe here, (1.) The singing of psalms and hymns is a gospel ordinance: it is an ordinance of God, and appointed for his glory. (2.) Though Christianity is an enemy to profane mirth, yet it encourages joy and gladness, and the proper expressions of these in the professors of it. God's people have reason to rejoice, and to sing for joy. They are to <hi type="italic">sing and to make melody in their hearts;</hi> not only with their voices, but with inward affection, and then their doing this will be as delightful and acceptable to God as music is to us: and it must be with a design to please him, and to promote his glory, that we do this; and then it will be done to the Lord. 4. Thanksgiving is another duty that the apostle exhorts to, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20">v. 20</reference>. We are appointed to sing psalms, &c., for the expression of our thankfulness to God; but, though we are not always singing, we should never want a disposition for this duty, as we never want matter for it. We must continue it throughout the whole course of our lives; and we should give thanks <hi type="italic">for all things;</hi> not only for spiritual blessings enjoyed, and eternal ones expected (for what of the former we have in hand, and for what of the other we have in hope), but for temporal mercies too; not only for our comforts, but also for our sanctified afflictions; not only for what immediately concerns ourselves, but for the instances of God's kindness and favour to others also. It is our duty in <hi type="italic">every thing to give thanks unto God and the Father,</hi> to God as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and our Father in him, in whose name we are to offer up all our prayers, and praises, and spiritual services, that they may be acceptable to God.
entries.51241d14c016b83392ca87162cf7c0f742b792a7: <div eID="gen31878" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Duties of Husbands and Wives. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31879" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God. <hi type="super">22</hi> Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord. <hi type="super">23</hi> For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body. <hi type="super">24</hi> Therefore as the church is subject unto Christ, so <hi type="italic">let</hi> the wives <hi type="italic">be</hi> to their own husbands in every thing. <hi type="super">25</hi> Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; <hi type="super">26</hi> That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, <hi type="super">27</hi> That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. <hi type="super">28</hi> So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself. <hi type="super">29</hi> For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church: <hi type="super">30</hi> For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones. 31 For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. 32 This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church. <hi type="super">33</hi> Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife <hi type="italic">see</hi> that she reverence <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband. <div eID="gen31879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31880" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle begins his exhortation to the discharge of relative duties. As a general foundation for these duties, he lays down that rule <reference osisRef="Eph.5.21">v. 21</reference>. There is a mutual submission that Christians owe one to another, condescending to bear one another's burdens: not advancing themselves above others, nor domineering over one another and giving laws to one another. Paul was an example of this truly Christian temper, for he <hi type="italic">became all things to all men.</hi> We must be of a yielding and of a submissive spirit, and ready to all the duties of the respective places and stations that God has allotted to us in the world. <hi type="italic">In the fear of God,</hi> that is, so far as is consistent with the fear of God, for his sake, and out of conscience towards him, and that hereby we may give proof that we truly fear him. Where there is this mutual condescension and submission, the duties of all relations will be the better performed. From <reference osisRef="Eph.5.22">v. 22</reference> to the end he speaks of the duties of husbands and wives; and he speaks of these in a Christian manner, setting the church as an example of the wife's subjection, and Christ as an example of love in husbands. <div eID="gen31880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31881" type="x-p"/> I. The duty prescribed to wives is submission to their husbands in the Lord (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.22">v. 22</reference>), which submission includes the honouring and obeying of them, and that from a principle of love to them. They must do this in compliance with God's authority, who has commanded it, which is doing it <hi type="italic">as unto the Lord;</hi> or it may be understood by way of similitude and likeness, so that the sense may be, "as, being devoted to God, you submit yourselves unto him." From the former sense we may learn that by a conscientious discharge of the duties we owe to our fellow-creatures we obey and please God himself; and, from the latter, that God not only requires and insists on those duties which immediately respect himself, but such as respect our neighbours too. The apostle assigns the reason of this submission from wives: <hi type="italic">For the husband is the head of the wife,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.23">v. 23</reference>. The metaphor is taken from the head in the natural body, which, being the seat of reason, of wisdom, and of knowledge, and the fountain of sense and motion, is more excellent than the rest of the body. God has given the man the pre-eminence and a right to direct and govern by creation, and in that original law of the relation, <hi type="italic">Thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.</hi> Whatever there is of uneasiness in this, it is an effect of sin coming into the world. Generally, too, the man has (what he ought to have) a superiority in wisdom and knowledge. He is therefore the head, <hi type="italic">even as Christ is the head of the church.</hi> There is a resemblance of Christ's authority over the church in that superiority and headship which God has appointed to the husband. The apostle adds, <hi type="italic">and he is the Saviour of the body.</hi> Christ's authority is exercised over the church for the saving of her from evil, and the supplying of her with every thing good for her. In like manner should the husband be employed for the protection and comfort of his spouse; and therefore she should the more cheerfully submit herself unto him. So it follows, <hi type="italic">Therefore as the church is subject unto Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.24">v. 24</reference>), with cheerfulness, with fidelity, with humility, <hi type="italic">so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing</hi>—in every thing to which their authority justly extends itself, in every thing lawful and consistent with duty to God. <div eID="gen31881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31882" type="x-p"/> II. The duty of husbands (on the other hand), is to love their wives (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.25">v. 25</reference>); for without this they would abuse their superiority and headship, and, wherever this prevails as it ought to do, it will infer the other duties of the relation, it being a special and peculiar affection that is required in her behalf. The love of Christ to the church is proposed as an example of this, which love of his is a sincere, a pure, an ardent, and constant affection, and that notwithstanding the imperfections and failures that she is guilty of. The greatness of his love to the church appeared in his giving himself unto the death for it. Observe, As the church's subjection to Christ is proposed as an exemplar to wives, so the love of Christ to his church is proposed as a pattern to husbands; and while such exemplars are offered to both, and so much is required of each, neither has reason to complain of the divine injunctions. The love which God requires from the husband in behalf of his wife will make amends for the subjection which he demands from her to her husband; and the prescribed subjection of the wife will be an abundant return for that love of the husband which God has made her due. The apostle, having mentioned Christ's love to the church, enlarges upon it, assigning the reason why he gave himself for it, namely, that he might sanctify it in this world, and glorify it in the next: <hi type="italic">That he might sanctify and cleanse it, with the washing of water by the word</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.26">v. 26</reference>)—that he might endue all his members with a principle of holiness, and deliver them from the guilt, the pollution, and the dominion of sin. The instrumental means whereby this is affected are the instituted sacraments, particularly the washing of baptism and the preaching and reception of the gospel. <hi type="italic">And that he might present it to himself,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">v. 27</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot thinks the apostle alludes here to the Jews' extraordinary carefulness in their washings for purification. They were careful that there should be no wrinkle to keep the flesh from the water, and no spot nor dirt which was not thoroughly washed. Others understand him as alluding to a garment come newly out of the fuller's hand, purged from spots, stretched from wrinkles, the former newly contracted, the latter by long time and custom. <hi type="italic">That he might present it to himself</hi>—that he might perfectly unite it to himself in the great day, <hi type="italic">a glorious church,</hi> perfect in knowledge and in holiness, <hi type="italic">not having spot, nor wrinkle, nor any such thing,</hi> nothing of deformity or defilement remaining, but being entirely amiable and pleasing in his eye, <hi type="italic">holy and without blemish,</hi> free from the least remains of sin. The church in general, and particular believers, will not be without spot or wrinkle till they come to glory. From <reference osisRef="Eph.5.26-Eph.5.27">this and the former verse</reference> together we may take notice that the glorifying of the church is intended in the sanctifying of it: and that those, and those only, who are sanctified now, will be glorified hereafter.—<hi type="italic">So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.5.28">v. 28</reference>. The wife being made one with her husband (not in a natural, but in a civil and in a relative sense), this is an argument why he should love her with as cordial and as ardent an affection as that which he loves himself. <hi type="italic">For no man ever yet hated his own flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.29">v. 29</reference>—(no man in his right senses ever hated himself, however deformed, or whatever his imperfections might be); so far from it that <hi type="italic">he nourishes and cherishes it;</hi> he uses himself with a great deal of care and tenderness, and is industrious to supply himself with every thing convenient or good for him, with food and clothing, &c. <hi type="italic">Even as the Lord the church:</hi> that is, as the Lord nourishes and cherishes the church, which he furnishes with all things that he sees needful or good for her, with whatever conduces to her everlasting happiness and welfare. The apostle adds, <hi type="italic">For we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.30">v. 30</reference>. He assigns this as a reason why Christ nourishes and cherishes his church—because all who belong to it <hi type="italic">are members of his body,</hi> that is, of his mystical body. Or, we are members <hi type="italic">out of his body:</hi> all the grace and glory which the church has are from Christ, as Eve was taken out of the man. But, as one observes, it being the manner of the sacred writings to express a complex body by the enumeration of its several parts, as the heaven and earth for the world, evening and morning for the natural day, so here, by body, flesh, and bones, we are to understand himself, the meaning of the verse being that we are members of Christ.—<hi type="italic">For this cause</hi> (because they are one, as Christ and his church are one) <hi type="italic">shall a man leave his father and mother;</hi> the apostle refers to the words of Adam, when Eve was given to him for a meet help, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.24">Gen. ii. 24</reference>. We are not to understand by this that a man's obligation to other relations is cancelled upon his marriage, but only that this relation is to be preferred to all others, there being a nearer union between these two than between any others, that the man must rather leave any of those than his wife.—<hi type="italic">And they two shall be one flesh,</hi> that is, by virtue of the matrimonial bond. <hi type="italic">This is a great mystery,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.32">v. 32</reference>. Those words of Adam, just mentioned by the apostle, are spoken literally of marriage; but they have also a hidden mystical sense in them, relating to the union between Christ and his church, of which the conjugal union between Adam and the mother of us all was a type: though not instituted or appointed by God to signify this, yet it was a kind of natural type, as having a resemblance to it: <hi type="italic">I speak concerning Christ and the church.</hi> <div eID="gen31882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31883" type="x-p"/> After this, the apostle concludes this part of his discourse with a brief summary of the duty of husbands and wives, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.33">v. 33</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Nevertheless</hi> (though there be such a secret mystical sense, yet the plain literal sense concerns you) <hi type="italic">let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself,</hi> with such a sincere, peculiar, singular, and prevailing affection as that is which he bears to himself. <hi type="italic">And the wife see that she reverence her husband.</hi>" Reverence consists of love and esteem, which produce a care to please, and of fear, which awakens a caution lest just offence be given. That the wife thus reverence her husband is the will of God and the law of the relation.  <chapter eID="Eph.5"/> <div eID="gen31883" type="x-p"/>

entries.c719228843bfd57ab7a5d6ce53e8d69446646bba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17667"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Eph.5.1-Eph.5.33">Ep 5:1-33</reference>. Exhortations to Love: And against Carnal Lusts and Communications. Circumspection in Walk: Redeeming the Time: Being Filled with the Spirit: Singing to the Lord with Thankfulness: The Wife's Duty to the Husband Rests on that of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen35690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17667"/><hi type="bold">1. therefore--</hi>seeing that "God in Christ forgave you" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.32">Ep 4:32</reference>).<div eID="gen35690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">followers--</hi>Greek, "imitators" of God, in respect to "love" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference>): God's essential character (<reference osisRef="1John.4.16">1Jo 4:16</reference>).<div eID="gen35691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as dear children--</hi>Greek, "as children beloved"; to which <reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference> refers, "As Christ also loved us" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.19">1Jo 4:19</reference>). "We are sons of men, when we do ill; sons of God, when we do well" [Augustine, on Psalm 52]; (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Mt 5:44</reference>, 45, 48). Sonship infers an absolute necessity of imitation, it being vain to assume the title of son without any similitude of the Father [Pearson]. <div eID="gen35692" type="x-p"/>
entries.fce96d9776b0dbfd6e98a91b2d865a6ee9fcae94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17668"/><div sID="gen35693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17668"/><hi type="bold">2. And--</hi>in proof that you are so.<div eID="gen35693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walk in love--</hi>resuming <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Ep 4:1</reference>, "walk worthy of the vocation."<div eID="gen35694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as Christ ... loved us--</hi>From the love of the Father he passes to the love of the Son, in whom God most endearingly manifests His love to us.<div eID="gen35695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given himself for us--</hi>Greek, "given Himself up (namely, to death, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>) for us," that is, in our behalf: not here vicarious substitution, though that is indirectly implied, "in our stead." The offerer, and the offering that He offered, were one and the same (<reference osisRef="John.15.13">Joh 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.8">Ro 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen35696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35697" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">offering and a sacrifice--</hi>"Offering" expresses generally His presenting Himself to the Father, as the Representative undertaking the cause of the whole of our lost race (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.6-Ps.40.8">Psa 40:6-8</reference>), including His life of obedience; though not excluding His offering of His body for us (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.10">He 10:10</reference>). It is usually an unbloody offering, in the more limited sense. "Sacrifice" refers to His death for us exclusively. Christ is here, in reference to <reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference> (quoted again in <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">He 10:5</reference>), represented as the antitype of all the offerings of the law, whether the unbloody or bloody, eucharistical or propitiatory.<div eID="gen35697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a sweet-smelling savour--</hi>Greek, "for an odor of a sweet smell," that is, God is well pleased with the offering on the ground of its sweetness, and so is reconciled to us (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2Co 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.6-Heb.10.17">He 10:6-17</reference>). The ointment compounded of principal spices, poured upon Aaron's head, answers to the variety of the graces by which He was enabled to "offer Himself a sacrifice for a sweet-smelling savor." Another type, or prophecy by figure, was "the sweet savor" ("savor of rest," Margin) which God smelled in Noah's sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Ge 8:21</reference>). Again, as what Christ is, believers also are (<reference osisRef="1John.4.17">1Jo 4:17</reference>), and ministers are: Paul says (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>) "we are unto God a sweet savor of Christ." <div eID="gen35698" type="x-p"/>
entries.32c83844a2bd2a946197e2fce34942e051b670d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17669"/><div sID="gen35699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17669"/><hi type="bold">3. once named--</hi>Greek, "Let it not be even named" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.4">Ep 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.12">12</reference>). "Uncleanness" and "covetousness" are taken up again from <reference osisRef="Eph.4.19">Ep 4:19</reference>. The two are so closely allied that the Greek for "covetousness" (pleonexia) is used sometimes in Scripture, and often in the Greek Fathers, for sins of impurity. The common principle is the longing to fill one's desire with material objects of sense, outside of God. The expression, "not be even named," applies better to impurity, than to "covetousness." <div eID="gen35699" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d37d9c7b99b62691ae277150642ea70933b0f0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17670"/><div sID="gen35700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17670"/><hi type="bold">4. filthiness--</hi>obscenity in act or gesture.<div eID="gen35700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foolish talking--</hi>the talk of fools, which is folly and sin together. The Greek of it, and of "filthiness," occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.<div eID="gen35701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor--</hi>rather, "or" (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>).<div eID="gen35702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">jesting--</hi>Greek, "eutrapelia"; found nowhere else in the New Testament: implying strictly that versatility which turns about and adapts itself, without regard to principle, to the shifting circumstances of the moment, and to the varying moods of those with whom it may deal. Not scurrile buffoonery, but refined "persiflage" and "badinage," for which Ephesus was famed [Plautus, A Boastful Soldier, 3.1,42-52], and which, so far from being censured, was and is thought by the world a pleasant accomplishment. In <reference osisRef="Col.3.8">Col 3:8</reference>, "filthy communication" refers to the foulness; "foolish talking," to the folly; "jesting," to the false refinement (and trifling witticism [Tittmann]) Of discourse unseasoned with the salt of grace [Trench].<div eID="gen35703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not convenient--</hi>"unseemly"; not such "as become saints" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>).<div eID="gen35704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rather giving of thanks--</hi>a happy play on sounds in Greek, "eucharistia" contrasted with "eutrapelia"; refined "jesting" and subtle humor sometimes offend the tender feelings of grace; "giving of thanks" gives that real cheerfulness of spirit to believers which the worldly try to get from "jesting" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">Ep 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jas 5:13</reference>). <div eID="gen35705" type="x-p"/>
entries.92b7424805cf5a492afe2cb83da04c36a8c85eb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17671"/><div sID="gen35706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17671"/><hi type="bold">5. this ye know--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "Of this ye are sure knowing"; or as Alford, "This ye know being aware."<div eID="gen35706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covetous ... idolater--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>). The best reading may be translated, That is to say, literally, which is (in other words) an idolater. Paul himself had forsaken all for Christ (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2Co 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.27">11:27</reference>). Covetousness is worship of the creature instead of the Creator, the highest treason against the King of kings (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">1Sa 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.24">Mt 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.15">1Jo 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen35707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath--</hi>The present implies the fixedness of the exclusion, grounded on the eternal verities of that kingdom [Alford].<div eID="gen35708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Christ and of God--</hi>rather, as one Greek article is applied to both, "of Christ and God," implying their perfect oneness, which is consistent only with the doctrine that Christ is God (compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.12">2Th 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21">1Ti 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">6:13</reference>). <div eID="gen35709" type="x-p"/>
entries.8afb791bd0d62bd6b42c7d64e1f0c320a89e3ff6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17672"/><div sID="gen35710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17672"/><hi type="bold">6. vain--</hi>empty, unreal words, namely, palliations of "uncleanness," <reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.20">Is 5:20</reference> (that it is natural to indulge in love), "covetousness" (that it is useful to society that men should pursue gain), and "jesting" (that it is witty and clever, and that God will not so severely punish for such things).<div eID="gen35710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of these things--</hi>uncleanness, covetousness, &c. (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.3-Eph.5.5">Ep 5:3-5</reference>).<div eID="gen35711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cometh--</hi>present, not merely "shall come." Is as sure as if already come.<div eID="gen35712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children--</hi>rather, "sons of disobedience" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>). The children of unbelief in doctrine (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.20">De 32:20</reference>) are "children of disobedience" in practice, and these again are "children of wrath." <div eID="gen35713" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa79f15f94d0f5c6b5e34b03935a76272eb0ff8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17673"/><div sID="gen35714" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17673"/>7. Here fellowship with wicked workers is forbidden; in <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Ep 5:11</reference>, with their wicked works. <div eID="gen35714" type="x-p"/>
entries.d07c614527d7d5ce9f76d6820f2fdc3d43c72088: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17674"/><div sID="gen35715" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17674"/><hi type="bold">8. sometimes--</hi>"once." The emphasis is on "were." Ye ought to have no fellowship with sin, which is darkness, for your state as darkness is now PAST. Stronger than "in darkness" (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.19">Ro 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen35715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">light--</hi>not merely "enlightened"; but light enlightening others (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.13">Ep 5:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>in union with the Lord, who is THE LIGHT.<div eID="gen35717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of light--</hi>not merely "of the light"; just as "children of disobedience" is used on the opposite side; those whose distinguishing characteristic is light. Pliny, a heathen writing to Trajan, bears unwilling testimony to the extraordinary purity of Christians' lives, contrasted with the people around them. <div eID="gen35718" type="x-p"/>
entries.af390010e7bde207b19f4b0da4ad79d29df10ea0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17675"/><div sID="gen35719" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17675"/><hi type="bold">9. fruit of the Spirit--</hi>taken by transcribers from <reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">Ga 5:22</reference>. The true reading is that of the oldest manuscripts, "The fruit of THE LIGHT"; in contrast with "the unfruitful works of darkness" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Ep 5:11</reference>). This verse is parenthetic. Walk as children of light, that is, in all good works and words, "FOR the fruit of the light is [borne] in [Alford; but Bengel, 'consists in'] all goodness [opposed to 'malice,' Ep 4:31], righteousness [opposed to 'covetousness,' Ep 5:3] and truth [opposed to 'lying,' Ep 4:25]." <div eID="gen35719" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f8972215470a6cbc737d2ae52085333ca4bc801: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17676"/><div sID="gen35720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17676"/><hi type="bold">10. Proving--</hi>construed with "walk" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Ep 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference>). As we prove a coin by the eye and the ear, and by using it, so by accurate and continued study, and above all by practice and experimental trial, we may prove or test "what is acceptable unto the Lord." This is the office of "light," of which believers are "children," to manifest what each thing is, whether sightly or unsightly. <div eID="gen35720" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7184f7ab4e9a14257b92a6f045816fcb22ccc1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17677"/><div sID="gen35721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17677"/><hi type="bold">11. unfruitful works of darkness--</hi>Sins are terminated in themselves, and therefore are called "works," not "fruits" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.19">Ga 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">22</reference>). Their only fruit is that which is not in a true sense fruit (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>), namely, "death" (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Ro 6:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Ga 6:8</reference>). Plants cannot bear "fruit" in the absence of light. Sin is "darkness," and its parent is the prince of darkness (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>). Graces, on the other hand, as flourishing in "the light," are reproductive, and abound in fruits; which, as harmoniously combining in one whole, are termed (in the singular) "the FRUIT of the Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.9">Ep 5:9</reference>).<div eID="gen35721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rather, &c.--</hi>Translate as Greek, "rather even reprove them" (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.5.14-Matt.5.16">Mt 5:14-16</reference>). Not only "have no fellowship, but even reprove them," namely, in words, and in your deeds, which, shining with "the light," virtually reprove all that is contrary to light (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.13">Ep 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.19-John.3.21">Joh 3:19-21</reference>). "Have no fellowship," does not imply that we can avoid all intercourse (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.10">1Co 5:10</reference>), but "avoid such fellowship as will defile yourselves"; just as light, though it touch filth, is not soiled by it; nay, as light detects it, so, "even reprove sin." <div eID="gen35722" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb6b01f5e7b15b41d2fa846d4083c6ea048fe4ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17678"/><div sID="gen35723" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17678"/>12. The Greek order is, "For the things done in secret by them, it is a shame even to speak of." The "for" gives his reason for "not naming" (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>) in detail the works of darkness, whereas he describes definitely (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.9">Ep 5:9</reference>) "the fruit of the light" [Bengel]. "Speak of," I think, is used here as "speaking of without reproving," in contrast to "even reprove them." Thus the "for" expresses this, Reprove them, for to speak of them without reproving them, is a shame (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>). Thus "works of darkness" answers to "things done in secret." <div eID="gen35723" type="x-p"/>
entries.56a136bbe038f2eb7d703486b21c3e5a0db71ffe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17679"/><div sID="gen35724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17679"/><hi type="bold">13. that are reproved--</hi>rather, "when they are reproved," namely, by you (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Ep 5:11</reference>).<div eID="gen35724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whatsoever doth make manifest--</hi>rather, "everything that is (that is, suffers itself to be) made manifest (or 'shone upon,' namely, by your 'reproving,' <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Ep 5:11</reference>) is (thenceforth no longer 'darkness,' <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Ep 5:8</reference>, but) light." The devil and the wicked will not suffer themselves to be made manifest by the light, but love darkness, though outwardly the light shines round them. Therefore, "light" has no transforming effect on them, so that they do not become light (<reference osisRef="John.3.19">Joh 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.20">20</reference>). But, says the apostle, you being now light yourselves (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Ep 5:8</reference>), by bringing to light through reproof those who are in darkness, will convert them to light. Your consistent lives and faithful reproofs will be your "armor of light" (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">Ro 13:12</reference>) in making an inroad on the kingdom of darkness. <div eID="gen35725" type="x-p"/>
entries.60cc0fa2d8f1d7495599979fa64a0a6440d5e954: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17680"/><div sID="gen35726" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17680"/><hi type="bold">14. Wherefore--</hi>referring to the whole foregoing argument (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Ep 5:8</reference>, 11, 13). Seeing that light (spiritual) dispels the pre-existing darkness, He (God) saith ... (compare the same phrase, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Ep 4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen35726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Awake--</hi>The reading of all the oldest manuscripts is "Up!" or, "Rouse thee!" a phrase used in stirring men to activity. The words are a paraphrase of <reference osisRef="Isa.60.1">Is 60:1</reference>, 2, not an exact quotation. The word "Christ," shows that in quoting the prophecy, he views it in the light thrown on it by its Gospel fulfilment. As Israel is called on to "awake" from its previous state of "darkness" and "death" (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.10">Is 59:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.2">60:2</reference>), for that her Light is come; so the Church, and each individual is similarly called to awake. Believers are called on to "awake" out of sleep; unbelievers, to "arise" from the dead (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.25.5">Mt 25:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.11">Ro 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.6">1Th 5:6</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">Ep 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen35727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ--</hi>"the true light," "the Sun of righteousness."<div eID="gen35728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give thee light--</hi>rather, as Greek, "shall shine upon thee" (so enabling thee by being "made manifest" to become, and be, by the very fact, "light," <reference osisRef="Eph.5.13">Ep 5:13</reference>; then being so "enlightened," <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>, thou shalt be able, by "reproving," to enlighten others). <div eID="gen35729" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5870429fffaaa5b38fea2852e15c763f0c47e2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17681"/><div sID="gen35730" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17681"/><hi type="bold">15. that--</hi>rather as Greek, "See how ye walk," &c. The double idea is compressed into one sentence: "See (take heed) how ye walk," and "See that ye walk circumspectly." The manner, as well as the act itself, is included. See how ye are walking, with a view to your being circumspect (literally, accurate, exact) in your walk. Compare <reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>, "Walk in wisdom (answering to 'as wise' here) toward them that are without" (answering to "circumspectly," that is, correctly, in relation to the unbelievers around, not giving occasion of stumbling to any, but edifying all by a consistent walk).<div eID="gen35730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not as fools--</hi>Greek, "not as unwise, but as wise." <div eID="gen35731" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe17598a899e7d9d5bd0f14011dbb73a3af05133: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17682"/><div sID="gen35732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17682"/><hi type="bold">16. Redeeming the time--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>). Greek, "Buying up for yourselves the seasonable time" (whenever it occurs) of good to yourselves and to others. Buying off from the vanities of "them that are without" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>), and of the "unwise" (here in Ephesians), the opportune time afforded to you for the work of God. In a narrower sense, special favorable seasons for good, occasionally presenting themselves, are referred to, of which believers ought diligently to avail themselves. This constitutes true "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">Ep 5:15</reference>). In a larger sense, the whole season from the time that one is spiritually awakened, is to be "redeemed" from vanity for God (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2Co 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.2-1Pet.4.4">1Pe 4:2-4</reference>). "Redeem" implies the preciousness of the opportune season, a jewel to be bought at any price. Wahl explains, "Redeeming for yourselves (that is, availing yourselves of) the opportunity (offered you of acting aright), and commanding the time as a master does his servant." Tittmann, "Watch the time, and make it your own so as to control it; as merchants look out for opportunities, and accurately choose out the best goods; serve not the time, but command it, and it shall do what you approve." So Pindar [Pythia, 4.509], "The time followed him as his servant, and was not as a runaway slave."<div eID="gen35732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because the days are evil--</hi>The days of life in general are so exposed to evil, as to make it necessary to make the most of the seasonable opportunity so long as it lasts (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">Ep 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.47.9">Ge 47:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.5">Psa 49:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ec 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.35">Joh 12:35</reference>). Besides, there are many special evil days (in persecution, sickness, &c.) when the Christian is laid by in silence; therefore he needs the more to improve the seasonable times afforded to him (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Am 5:13</reference>), which Paul perhaps alludes to. <div eID="gen35733" type="x-p"/>
entries.7680936833ebb1feb64f53bea1633b5175c60754: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17683"/><div sID="gen35734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17683"/><hi type="bold">17. Wherefore--</hi>seeing that ye need to walk so circumspectly, choosing and using the right opportunity of good.<div eID="gen35734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unwise--</hi>a different Greek word from that in <reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">Ep 5:15</reference>. Translate, "foolish," or "senseless."<div eID="gen35735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35736" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understanding--</hi>not merely knowing as a matter of fact (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.47">Lu 12:47</reference>), but knowing with understanding.<div eID="gen35736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the will of the Lord--</hi>as to how each opportunity is to be used. The Lord's will, ultimately, is our "sanctification" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.3">1Th 4:3</reference>); and that "in every thing," meantime, we should "give thanks" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.18">1Th 5:18</reference>; compare above, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.10">Ep 5:10</reference>). <div eID="gen35737" type="x-p"/>
entries.88933c92e1640e0cf331b7d27868d20a8530b99e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17684"/><div sID="gen35738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17684"/><hi type="bold">18. excess--</hi>worthless, ruinous, reckless prodigality.<div eID="gen35738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein--</hi>not in the wine itself when used aright (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1Ti 5:23</reference>), but in the "excess" as to it.<div eID="gen35739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but be filled with the Spirit--</hi>The effect in inspiration was that the person was "filled" with an ecstatic exhilaration, like that caused by wine; hence the two are here connected (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.13-Acts.2.18">Ac 2:13-18</reference>). Hence arose the abstinence from wine of many of the prophets, for example, John the Baptist, namely, in order to keep distinct before the world the ecstasy caused by the Spirit, from that caused by wine. So also in ordinary Christians the Spirit dwells not in the mind that seeks the disturbing influences of excitement, but in the well-balanced prayerful mind. Such a one expresses his joy, not in drunken or worldly songs, but in Christian hymns of thankfulness. <div eID="gen35740" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f49ef813191aba4242adea6e4f33046468938ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17685"/><div sID="gen35741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17685"/>19. (<reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen35741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to yourselves--</hi>"to one another." Hence soon arose the antiphonal or responsive chanting of which Pliny writes to Trajan: "They are wont on a fixed day to meet before daylight [to avoid persecution] and to recite a hymn among themselves by turns, to Christ, as if being God." The Spirit gives true eloquence; wine, a spurious eloquence.<div eID="gen35742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">psalms--</hi>generally accompanied by an instrument.<div eID="gen35743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hymns--</hi>in direct praise to God (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.16.25">Ac 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.26">1Co 14:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jas 5:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">songs--</hi>the general term for lyric pieces; "spiritual" is added to mark their being here restricted to sacred subjects, though not merely to direct praises of God, but also containing exhortations, prophecies, &c. Contrast the drunken "songs," <reference osisRef="Amos.8.10">Am 8:10</reference>.<div eID="gen35745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">making melody--</hi>Greek, "playing and singing with an instrument."<div eID="gen35746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in your heart--</hi>not merely with the tongue; but the serious feeling of the heart accompanying the singing of the lips (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.15">1Co 14:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.47.7">Psa 47:7</reference>). The contrast is between the heathen and the Christian practice, "Let your songs be not the drinking songs of heathen feasts, but psalms and hymns; and their accompaniment, not the music of the lyre, but the melody of the heart" [Conybeare and Howson].<div eID="gen35747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the Lord--</hi>See Pliny's letter quoted above: "To Christ as God." <div eID="gen35748" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3c708aa592066559cf8e2f6bee43b5910071ec7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17686"/><div sID="gen35749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17686"/><hi type="bold">20. thanks ... for all things--</hi>even for adversities; also for blessings, unknown as well as known (<reference osisRef="Col.3.17">Col 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.18">1Th 5:18</reference>).<div eID="gen35749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto God and the Father--</hi>the Fountain of every blessing in Creation, Providence, Election, and Redemption.<div eID="gen35750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>by whom all things, even distresses, become ours (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.35">Ro 8:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">37</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.20-1Cor.3.23">1Co 3:20-23</reference>). <div eID="gen35751" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc5d30e7fb579dd97552f421d589f233d611e431: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17687"/><div sID="gen35752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17687"/>21. (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.3">Php 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5">1Pe 5:5</reference>.) Here he passes from our relations to God, to those which concern our fellow men.<div eID="gen35752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the fear of God--</hi>All the oldest manuscripts and authorities read, "in the fear of Christ." The believer passes from under the bondage of the law as a letter, to be "the servant of Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>), which, through the instinct of love to Him, is really to be "the Lord's freeman"; for he is "under the law to Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.21">1Co 9:21</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.8.36">Joh 8:36</reference>). Christ, not the Father (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>), is to be our judge. Thus reverential fear of displeasing Him is the motive for discharging our relative duties as Christians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.22">1Co 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">2Co 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.13">1Pe 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen35753" type="x-p"/>
entries.622d01cb1e82ab5ee79e26e47c777c008eb5186a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17688"/><div sID="gen35754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17688"/>22. (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.9">Ep 6:9</reference>.) The Church's relation to Christ in His everlasting purpose, is the foundation and archetype of the three greatest of earthly relations, that of husband and wife (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.22-Eph.5.33">Ep 5:22-33</reference>), parent and child (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.1-Eph.6.4">Ep 6:1-4</reference>), master and servant (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.4-Eph.6.9">Ep 6:4-9</reference>). The oldest manuscripts omit "submit yourselves"; supplying it from <reference osisRef="Eph.5.21">Ep 5:21</reference>, "Ye wives (submitting yourselves) unto your own husbands." "Your own" is an argument for submissiveness on the part of the wives; it is not a stranger, but your own husbands whom you are called on to submit unto (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Ge 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2">1Co 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">14:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.18">Col 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.5">Tit 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.1-1Pet.3.7">1Pe 3:1-7</reference>). Those subject ought to submit themselves, of whatever kind their superiors are. "Submit" is the term used of wives: "obey," of children (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.1">Ep 6:1</reference>), as there is a greater equality between wives and husbands, than between children and parents.<div eID="gen35754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as unto the Lord--</hi>Submissiveness is rendered by the wife to the husband under the eye of Christ, and so is rendered to Christ Himself.
